skills.desc: Integrate the Users plugin into a NocoBase App, build a user management page on its API and configure its permissions, or add an application-owned role scope through the public Server contracts.
skills.body:
---
name: nocobase-app-plugin-users
description: Integrate the Users plugin into a NocoBase App, build a user management page on its API and configure its permissions, or add an application-owned role scope through the public Server contracts.
metadata:
  short-description: Integrate reusable user administration
---

# User Management App Plugin

Use this Skill when an application needs user management, or when another
plugin needs to expose application-specific roles in user management. Do
not use it to modify the Users plugin source or to replace Authentication's
user, account, or Session storage.

## Public surfaces

- Client registration factory and `UsersClientOptions`:
  `@nocobase/app-plugin-users/client`. It contributes only the public
  invitation page at `/invite/:token`; there is no user management page.
- Typed API client: `UsersClient` and its types from
  `@nocobase/app-plugin-users/client/user-client`.
- Server contracts: `userManagementServiceToken`,
  `userRoleScopeRegistryToken`, `UserRoleScope`, and related types from
  `@nocobase/app-plugin-users/server/tokens`.
- HTTP API: `GET /api/users` (`page`, `pageSize`, `q`, `status`, `roleScope`, `role`, `sort=name`, `order=asc|desc`; answers `{ data, meta: { page, pageSize, total } }`), `GET /api/users/options`, `GET /api/users/:userId` (latest managed profile and role scopes, requires `user/read`, 404 for absent accounts), `POST /api/users`, `PATCH /api/users/:userId`, `DELETE /api/users/:userId?confirm=true`, `POST /api/users/:userId/disable|enable|resetPassword|revokeSessions`, and `PUT /api/users/:userId/roleScopes/:scope`. The running application documents each one, with request and response schemas, at `/api/swagger/docs` (JSON at `/api/swagger`) under the `Users` tag. Failures use the standard error body; branch on `error.reason`, such as `USER_NOT_FOUND`, `SELF_DELETE_NOT_ALLOWED`, `LAST_ASSIGNMENT` or `USER_EMAIL_CONFLICT`.

`UsersClient.update(userId, { name?, username?, email?, roleScopes? })` supports one atomic editor Save. Profile fields require `update`; submitted `roleScopes` additionally require `assign-role`. A roles-only payload requires `assign-role` without `update`. The service validates scope values, runs each applicable target-account guard, and commits profile changes and all submitted scope replacements in the caller-owned transaction, notifying permission clients only after commit. Omitted scopes are preserved. Keep the existing per-scope PUT for callers needing only one scope. Do not implement a combined Save as sequential profile and role requests: a later failure would leave a partially saved account.

Every HTTP route requires Authentication and Authorization. Routes check the `user` record type with the applicable action from `read`, `create`, `update`, `disable`, `enable`, `assign-role`, `reset-password`, `revoke-sessions` or `delete`. Account creation checks both `create` and `assign-role`. `delete` is permitted only while an application role scope can clean a deleted user up.

## Register the plugin

1. Register Authentication, Authorization, and then Users in the App's Client
   and Server plugin arrays. The Client factory takes no placement options:
   `users()`.
2. Grant only the `user` actions those roles need, on `{ type: 'user', id: '*' }` because `user` is a record type. The plugin creates no roles and grants no access by itself.
3. For a user management page, build it in the App on `UsersClient` and declare it among the App's own routes with the page access it needs; the plugin ships none.

The invitation page reports results through `useToaster()` from `@nocobase/app-client`, so the App needs the `@nocobase/app-client` that exports it and registers a toaster service, as the templates do: `client/lib/toaster.ts` from the template, and `this.app.container.instance(toasterToken, createToaster())` in the `register()` of `client/service-provider.ts`, with the `Toaster` component mounted in `client/react-providers.ts`. Without the registration nothing throws, but its toasts are only logged to the browser console.

The default `app` permission-set scope is supplied by Users whenever the Authorization plugin's `authorizationToken` is available. Do not copy a user-roles Provider into an application. Set `users.permissionSets: false` to replace the default with an application-owned scope.

## Add an application role scope

Resolve `userRoleScopeRegistryToken` in an application or business plugin
ServiceProvider and register one `UserRoleScope` during `boot()`. The scope owns
its available options, current assignment lookup, role filtering, atomic
replacement, and any disable guard. Unregister it during `shutdown()`.

Use the `DatabaseConnection` passed to each scope method. This is the
caller-owned transaction used to keep account creation or state changes atomic
with role assignments. Do not open an unrelated transaction and do not write
Authentication's internal tables.

Guard who may act on whom with `assertCanAdminister(userId, actorId, action, connection)`: the management API calls it for `update`, `disable`, `enable`, `reset-password`, `revoke-sessions` and `assign-role` with the authenticated actor, in the action's transaction and before anything changes, after authorization of the action itself has passed. Throw a `UserRoleScopeError` to refuse, for example when someone who is not an application owner resets an owner's password; the route answers `FAILED_PRECONDITION` with the scope's reason. Service callers that pass no `actorId` are the application's own server-side work and are not asked. Deletion has its own `assertCanDelete(userId, actorId, connection)`.

For a required single-role scope, set `selection: 'single'` and
`requiredOnCreate: true`. Reject invalid values in the scope and enforce
business invariants such as the last-administrator rule on the server.

Set `assignable: false` or `removable: false` on an option when user management
must show a protected assignment but must not add or revoke it. Enforce the
same rule in `replace()` because these flags only control the Client. Set
`hasAuthenticatedDefaultAccess: true` when the scope lists direct assignments
but all signed-in users also inherit separately configured default access, so a
user management page can explain that distinction instead of treating the
default as a role.
Use `labelI18nKey` with `labelI18nNs` on a scope or option when its owner has
registered Client locale resources; keep `label` as the readable fallback.
Implement optional `getMany()` when assignments can be read as a batch. Users
uses it for list pages and falls back to `get()` for existing scopes.

## Invite users

Holders of `invite` on `user` can create invitations through `POST /api/users/invitations` or `UsersClient`; choosing roles also requires `assign-role`. Results include a shareable link even when email succeeds. A queued invitation closed or rotated by another request returns `emailSent=false` without a link, while the other recipients still complete. Original inviters can renew with `sendEmail=false`, which invalidates the old link. Plugin-specific invitations must use their domain endpoint, which rechecks its own grants. Other managers may resend email but receive no link. Tokens last seven days; only hashes are stored. Each invitation has one email language: `locale` when given (it must be an application language, otherwise `INVALID_INVITATION`), else the caller's interface language when offered, else the application default. It is stored on the invitation, reused by resends and returned by the lookup; the accept page opens in it, and accepting stores the page's language as the new account's `i18n.locale`. Plugin domains that invite through `UserManagementService.invite` pass `locale` and the caller's request locale as `inviterLocale`.

New accounts register directly from the invitation link with a name and password; acceptance leaves `emailVerified=false`. Email delivery is optional: authorized original inviters can privately forward the link when the email channel is absent or fails. Links use `app.publicOrigin` when configured, otherwise the invitation request origin. Existing accounts must sign in with the invited email. Acceptance consumes only the supplied invitation and applies only its grants; handlers run in its transaction and roll back account creation on failure.

## Ownership

- Authentication owns user identity, credentials, account state, password
  hashing, and Sessions.
- Authorization owns Permission Sets, grants, and assignments.
- Users owns the management API, the invitation page, orchestration transaction,
  `user` authorization handler, and role-scope registry.
- The App or business plugin owns role definitions, role grants, assignments,
  the user management page, and role-specific invariants.
- The plugin's `skills/` source is authoritative. `.agents/skills/` is a
  synchronized copy and must not be edited.

## Permissions and constraints

- Browser route access is only navigation control. The Server independently
  authenticates and authorizes every request.
- A conditional grant is not accepted as an unrestricted user-management
  grant; use explicit static grants for this resource.
- Disabled users are rejected by Authentication and lose their existing HTTP
  Sessions and Realtime connections.
- Password hashes, Session tokens, reset tokens, and submitted passwords are
  never returned by the service or included in security events.

## Verification

- Anonymous API requests return `401`; authenticated requests without the
  requested `user` action return `403`.
- Creating a user with a required role scope creates both records, while role
  assignment failure rolls back the user.
- Duplicate emails or usernames return a stable `409` conflict. Password reset
  and database Session revocation commit or roll back together.
- Disabling a user invalidates HTTP Sessions and Realtime connections; enabling
  the user requires a new login.
- Role changes become visible after transaction commit and do not alter
  assignments outside the registered scope.
- The target App passes its relevant tests, typecheck, and build. Skill
  synchronization alone proves only that the copy matches this source.

Deletion uses `DELETE /api/users/:userId?confirm=true` and `user/delete` authorization. Obtain an explicit user deletion request before calling it. Application role scopes can guard deletion and clean dependent credentials transactionally. Historical user identities are retained but cannot sign in or appear in management lists.

Invitation emails use `notificationService.sendTransient()` so credentials never enter notification message snapshots or job storage. This performs one bounded attempt without durable retries or deduplication. Failures retain safe status/category diagnostics without raw provider messages. The inviter can generate and privately deliver a new link if delivery fails. Historical notification snapshots are not rewritten.

## Creation defaults and existing applications

Apply an option scope’s `defaultValue` only when creating a new account. An explicit empty array takes precedence; editing uses saved roles and never reapplies defaults. Member is a visible direct role that can be removed. A roleless person retains authenticated account basics but no role-granted business access. Upgrade Authentication, Authorization, and Users together, stop old writers before applying database tasks, and merge the template user pages and translations separately: upgrading plugins does not replace application-owned source. The new Authorization seed preserves existing users before removing Member’s global assignment; never recreate that assignment in application seeds or startup reconciliation.

## Invitation email

Prefer application `mailers`, optionally selected by `users.invitations.mailer`. Selection is explicit mailer, explicit legacy emailChannel, mailers.default, then implicit system-email. The new path needs no Notification installation; legacy sendTransient retains no-record/no-retry behavior. Users stops new invitation work, closes its own sender and waits for sends in parallel; it waits through invitation bookkeeping before the database closes. A timed-out invitation retains its real in-flight slot and is never automatically resent. The outer application shutdown budget remains `APP_SHUTDOWN_TIMEOUT_MS`. Declare mailers with `defineMailersConfig` and explicit `mailerEnvironment` mappings from `@nocobase/app-server/mailers/config`; restart after changing senders. Existing invitation permissions, tokens, share links and manual resend remain unchanged.

## User language preferences

The users Client plugin automatically integrates with `useAppLocale()` through the optional `AppLocalePreferenceContext` from `@nocobase/app-client`. Explicit selections store a JSON string at `i18n.locale` in `userPreferences`. Restore a validated server value before browser cache; if absent or unsupported, use the application default without saving it. Do not migrate unowned legacy browser locales into an account. Anonymous choices remain separate, and identity transitions invalidate old locale operations, including when Authorization remounts providers.

For recipient-language jobs, import `resolveUserLocale` and `userPreferencesServiceToken` from `@nocobase/app-plugin-users/server` and `i18nToken` from `@nocobase/app-server/i18n`. Call `resolveUserLocale(container.resolve(userPreferencesServiceToken), container.resolve(i18nToken), userId)`: a supported string preference wins, then a supported application default, then `en-US`. Load that locale with `ensureLocaleLoaded` before calling `getFixedT(namespace, locale)`. Do not derive durable language from a request session or `Accept-Language`; request negotiation remains session `locale`, header, then default. The package README contains the complete example and cache compatibility notes.

Service callers that pass no `actorId` are the application's own server-side work and are not asked. Deletion has its own `assertCanDelete(userId, actorId, connection)`.

For a required single-role scope, set `selection: 'single'` and
`requiredOnCreate: true`. Reject invalid values in the scope and enforce
business invariants such as the last-administrator rule on the server.

Set `assignable: false` or `removable: false` on an option when user management
must show a protected assignment but must not add or revoke it. Enforce the
same rule in `replace()` because these flags only control the Client. Set
`hasAuthenticatedDefaultAccess: true` when the scope lists direct assignments
but all signed-in users also inherit separately configured default access, so a
user management page can explain that distinction instead of treating the
default as a role.
Use `labelI18nKey` with `labelI18nNs` on a scope or option when its owner has
registered Client locale resources; keep `label` as the readable fallback.
Implement optional `getMany()` when assignments can be read as a batch. Users
uses it for list pages and falls back to `get()` for existing scopes.

## Invite users

Holders of `invite` on `user` can create invitations through `POST /api/users/invitations` or `UsersClient`; choosing roles also requires `assign-role`. Results include a shareable link even when email succeeds. A queued invitation closed or rotated by another request returns `emailSent=false` without a link, while the other recipients still complete. Original inviters can renew with `sendEmail=false`, which invalidates the old link. Plugin-specific invitations must use their domain endpoint, which rechecks its own grants. Other managers may resend email but receive no link. Tokens last seven days; only hashes are stored. Each invitation has one email language: `locale` when given (it must be an application language, otherwise `INVALID_INVITATION`), else the caller's interface language when offered, else the application default. It is stored on the invitation, reused by resends and returned by the lookup; the accept page opens in it, and accepting stores the page's language as the new account's `i18n.locale`. Plugin domains that invite through `UserManagementService.invite` pass `locale` and the caller's request locale as `inviterLocale`.

New accounts register directly from the invitation link with a name and password; acceptance leaves `emailVerified=false`. Email delivery is optional: authorized original inviters can privately forward the link when the email channel is absent or fails. Links use `app.publicOrigin` when configured, otherwise the invitation request origin. Existing accounts must sign in with the invited email. Acceptance consumes only the supplied invitation and applies only its grants; handlers run in its transaction and roll back account creation on failure.

## Ownership

- Authentication owns user identity, credentials, account state, password
  hashing, and Sessions.
- Authorization owns Permission Sets, grants, and assignments.
- Users owns the management API, the invitation page, orchestration transaction,
  `user` authorization handler, and role-scope registry.
- The App or business plugin owns role definitions, role grants, assignments,
  the user management page, and role-specific invariants.
- The plugin's `skills/` source is authoritative. `.agents/skills/` is a
  synchronized copy and must not be edited.

## Permissions and constraints

- Browser route access is only navigation control. The Server independently
  authenticates and authorizes every request.
- A conditional grant is not accepted as an unrestricted user-management
  grant; use explicit static grants for this resource.
- Disabled users are rejected by Authentication and lose their existing HTTP
  Sessions and Realtime connections.
- Password hashes, Session tokens, reset tokens, and submitted passwords are
  never returned by the service or included in security events.

## Verification

- Anonymous API requests return `401`; authenticated requests without the
  requested `user` action return `403`.
- Creating a user with a required role scope creates both records, while role
  assignment failure rolls back the user.
- Duplicate emails or usernames return a stable `409` conflict. Password reset
  and database Session revocation commit or roll back together.
- Disabling a user invalidates HTTP Sessions and Realtime connections; enabling
  the user requires a new login.
- Role changes become visible after transaction commit and do not alter
  assignments outside the registered scope.
- The target App passes its relevant tests, typecheck, and build. Skill
  synchronization alone proves only that the copy matches this source.

Deletion uses `DELETE /api/users/:userId?confirm=true` and `user/delete` authorization. Obtain an explicit user deletion request before calling it. Application role scopes can guard deletion and clean dependent credentials transactionally. Historical user identities are retained but cannot sign in or appear in management lists.

Invitation emails use `notificationService.sendTransient()` so credentials never enter notification message snapshots or job storage. This performs one bounded attempt without durable retries or deduplication. Failures retain safe status/category diagnostics without raw provider messages. The inviter can generate and privately deliver a new link if delivery fails. Historical notification snapshots are not rewritten.

## Creation defaults and existing applications

Apply an option scope’s `defaultValue` only when creating a new account. An explicit empty array takes precedence; editing uses saved roles and never reapplies defaults. Member is a visible direct role that can be removed. A roleless person retains authenticated account basics but no role-granted business access. Upgrade Authentication, Authorization, and Users together, stop old writers before applying database tasks, and merge the template user pages and translations separately: upgrading plugins does not replace application-owned source. The new Authorization seed preserves existing users before removing Member’s global assignment; never recreate that assignment in application seeds or startup reconciliation.

## Invitation email

Prefer application `mailers`, optionally selected by `users.invitations.mailer`. Selection is explicit mailer, explicit legacy emailChannel, mailers.default, then implicit system-email. The new path needs no Notification installation; legacy sendTransient retains no-record/no-retry behavior. Users stops new invitation work, closes its own sender and waits for sends in parallel; it waits through invitation bookkeeping before the database closes. A timed-out invitation retains its real in-flight slot and is never automatically resent. The outer application shutdown budget remains `APP_SHUTDOWN_TIMEOUT_MS`. Declare mailers with `defineMailersConfig` and explicit `mailerEnvironment` mappings from `@nocobase/app-server/mailers/config`; restart after changing senders. Existing invitation permissions, tokens, share links and manual resend remain unchanged.

## User language preferences

The users Client plugin automatically integrates with `useAppLocale()` through the optional `AppLocalePreferenceContext` from `@nocobase/app-client`. Explicit selections store a JSON string at `i18n.locale` in `userPreferences`. Restore a validated server value before browser cache; if absent or unsupported, use the application default without saving it. Do not migrate unowned legacy browser locales into an account. Anonymous choices remain separate, and identity transitions invalidate old locale operations, including when Authorization remounts providers.

For recipient-language jobs, import `resolveUserLocale` and `userPreferencesServiceToken` from `@nocobase/app-plugin-users/server` and `i18nToken` from `@nocobase/app-server/i18n`. Call `resolveUserLocale(container.resolve(userPreferencesServiceToken), container.resolve(i18nToken), userId)`: a supported string preference wins, then a supported application default, then `en-US`. Load that locale with `ensureLocaleLoaded` before calling `getFixedT(namespace, locale)`. Do not derive durable language from a request session or `Accept-Language`; request negotiation remains session `locale`, header, then default. The package README contains the complete example and cache compatibility notes.

skills.body:
---
name: nocobase-app-installer
description: Deploy a built NocoBase 3 application locally or over SSH to an offline Linux server, for production, with `@nocobase/app-installer` from the deployment archive `pnpm build --tar` writes, then upgrade, roll back and check it. Use when the user asks to deploy an application to production or a server, to upgrade or roll back such an installation, or when the directory holds an `installer.json` written by app-installer. Not for creating a project to develop, which is the `nocobase-create-app` Skill.
---

# Install and run NocoBase 3 with app-installer

This Skill installs NocoBase that is already built — nothing on the machine is developed, only run. `@nocobase/app-installer` puts each release under `releases/<version>_<build time>/app` and runs it under pm2; `config.yml`, `app.env`, `storage/`, `backups/` and `logs/` sit beside the releases and survive every upgrade. It installs from `--archive`, a deployment archive built in an application project. This Skill decides when to use it and how to act on what it reports; `--help` is the reference for every flag.

## Run it

Run the installer on the machine where the Agent works, with the registry named and `--json`. For SSH deployment this is the local machine, not the server:

```bash
npx --yes --registry="${NOCOBASE_REGISTRY:-https://registry.npmjs.org}" @nocobase/app-installer@beta <command> … --json
```

Use `@beta` for the published installer; do not fall back to an untagged invocation or `@latest`. Preserve an explicit version required for an existing installation or requested by the user, and use the snapshot tag when testing an unreleased local registry.

NocoBase 3 publishes to the public npm registry. `NOCOBASE_REGISTRY` is set only when someone points the shell at another registry, such as an unreleased snapshot; the installer records the registry in `installer.json` and suggests commands from it. The `--yes` before the package is npx's own: it downloads the installer without asking. The installer's `--yes`, after the command, is a separate answer that only the user gives.

Use the published `beta` channel unless the user specifies an exact version. An unreleased snapshot registry tags its packages `latest`; use that tag only when testing such a registry. Check `--help` before deploying to confirm the selected version supports `deploy` and `--ssh`.

`--json` prints one document on stdout and progress on stderr, in the same envelope as `pnpm nocobase … --json`. Read the document, not the exit code alone: `ok`, `status` (`success`, `success-noop` or `failure`), `result`, and on failure `error.code`, `error.message`, `error.suggestions` and `error.details`. Each suggestion has a `message` and, where there is one, a `run` of `{ command, args }`: an executable and its arguments, run as given without a shell. app-installer 0.1.0-beta.1 and earlier, which a suggested command pinned to that version still runs, print `status` `error` and `run` as one shell line that runs as printed, so tell success from failure by `ok`.

| Exit | Meaning                                                                                  |
| ---- | ---------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| `0`  | Done, or nothing to do (`success-noop`).                                                 |
| `1`  | Failed; an application that was already running was not touched.                        |
| `2`  | Invalid usage, a failed precheck, or a confirmation still needed; nothing was written.  |
| `3`  | An upgrade failed after switching and was rolled back; the previous release is running.  |
| `4`  | Rolling back failed too; the application is down.                                        |

## Choose the route

A project is source code someone changes, created by `nocobase-create-app` and developed locally; an installation is a built NocoBase that only runs, made by this Skill, usually in production. Settle the route before installing anything:

| The user asks to                                         | Route                                                                                                       |
| -------------------------------------------------------- | ----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| Install, create or try NocoBase, to develop with         | The `nocobase-create-app` Skill                                                                             |
| Deploy an application to production or a server          | This Skill, `--archive`, from the application's deployment archive                                          |
| Run it with Docker                                       | The application's `nocobase-deployment` Skill and Docker configuration                                     |

- "Install NocoBase on this server" with no project and no archive is not settled yet. Running the user's own application means creating it locally with `nocobase-create-app`, building its archive, and installing that here with `--archive`. Do not create a project on the server and run it with `pnpm dev`: that is development mode, not a deployment.
- An `installer.json` whose `source.kind` is `template` was installed from the published Hub template by an earlier app-installer. The current one refuses it with `STATE_UNSUPPORTED`; leave it to the app-installer version that installed it.
- When the working directory already holds `installer.json`, the installation exists: start with `status`.

## Choose where the installer runs

When the user supplies an SSH server, keep the Agent, this Skill and the installer on the local machine. Read [Remote deployment](references/remote-deployment.md) before proceeding: it covers local orchestration, offline execution and recovery. The server needs no Agent, Skill or npm access. The `install`, `status`, `upgrade` and `rollback` guidance below still defines the lifecycle; run remote operations with the same SSH options and absolute remote `--dir`.

When the Agent is already on the application server, use the local commands below. An archive is built where the sources are, not in the production installation. If the source project is available locally, follow its `AGENTS.md` and `nocobase-deployment` Skill to build; otherwise obtain the archive from the user or CI. Do not build or run a development project on the production server.

## Build the archive

In the application project, whose own `AGENTS.md` and `nocobase-deployment` Skill are the authority on building:

```bash
APP_BASE_PATH=/crm pnpm build --target linux-x64 --node-version 24 --tar
```

- `--target` and `--node-version` describe the machine that will run it, not the one building it: `node -p "process.platform + '-' + process.arch"` and `node --version` there; Alpine takes a `-musl` target. The installer refuses an archive built for another machine and names the command that fits.
- `APP_BASE_PATH` is compiled into the client, `/main` when unset. The application is served there, and every later archive must be built for the same one.
- A database other than SQLite needs its driver in the project before the build, such as `pnpm add @nocobase/db-postgres@beta`: an archive carries only the drivers it was built with.

The archive is `storage/exports/dist.tar.gz`; the user copies it to the machine that runs NocoBase, for example `scp storage/exports/dist.tar.gz user@server:/tmp/crm.tar.gz`. `ARCHIVE_TOO_OLD` or `STORAGE_IN_RELEASE` means the project's NocoBase packages are older than the installer needs: upgrade them, build again, then retry.

## Install

### Every installation

1. Check the machine: `node --version` (24 or later) and `command -v pm2`, which finds pm2 without starting its daemon. pm2 4.3 or later has to be installed globally, `npm install -g pm2`; a copy fetched through `npx` breaks `pm2 startup`. Report what is missing with the command that installs it, and install nothing globally unless the user asks. On Windows, work in WSL.
2. Settle with the user: the target directory, new or empty, such as `/srv/nocobase/crm`; the public origin without the base path, such as `https://apps.example.com`, which may be left out for a machine reached only at `http://127.0.0.1:<port>`; whether a reverse proxy sits in front; the port, 13000 by default and different for every installation on the machine; and the database, SQLite by default.
3. It listens on `127.0.0.1`, which suits a reverse proxy on the same machine; when people reach it directly at `http://<address>:<port>`, add `--host 0.0.0.0` and use that address as the origin. For another database add `--dialect <dialect>`, the connection as `--set database.connections.main.host=…` and friends, and the password as `--set-from-env database.connections.main.password=<VARIABLE>` after the user has exported it; never put a password on the command line.
4. `PORT_IN_USE` names a free port in `error.details.freePort`; offer it rather than picking one silently.

### Run it

`install <dir> --archive <file> --origin <origin> --json`. It needs no pnpm, and finishes in a minute or two. The archive must carry the driver for `--dialect`, or the install stops with `DRIVER_MISSING` and the build command that fixes it.

### When it succeeds

When `result.started` is true, the installation answered its health check. Tell the user:

- `result.url`, and the first sign-in: `result.initialAdmin.username` or its `email`, with the password under `users.initialAdmin` in `config.yml`. When `result.initialAdmin.defaultPassword` is true, that password is still the `admin123` from `config.example.yml` and has to be changed after signing in; otherwise it is the one they set. The result never carries the password, and `config.yml` stays unread;
- each command in `result.nextCommands`: `pm2 startup` prints a command they run once with sudo, after which pm2 restores the process list the installer saved, so the installation comes back after a reboot;
- with a reverse proxy: it forwards to the installation's port with the WebSocket upgrade headers. Several installations behind one origin are routed by their base paths;
- anything in `warnings`.

A failed install before the switch leaves the target as it found it. What the failing step said is in `error.details`: `output` for unpacking the release, `stderr` and `stdout` when the release's own CLI printed no result; a failure that CLI reports itself keeps the CLI's own code, such as `CONFIG_INVALID`, and its `error.message` and `error.suggestions` say what was wrong. `START_FAILED` means installed but not running: show `error.details.log`.

## Several installations on one machine

Each application is installed once, in a directory of its own, with its own `--port`. The pm2 process name defaults to `nocobase-<directory name>`, so directories with different names never collide; two directories with the same name report `PM2_NAME_IN_USE` before anything is written, and `--name` gives the second its own.

## Status

`status --dir <root> --json` changes nothing. Report the application and `version`, `current` (the release id), `endpoints.url`, `health.ok`, `process`, and anything in `warnings`. `node.matches: false` means the machine's Node major changed since the release was built, and it will not load its native modules until a release built for this machine replaces it: the warning names the steps — a rebuilt archive and `upgrade --archive` — which go through the same stop, backup and confirmation as any upgrade. A non-null `pending` means an operation was interrupted; see below.

## Upgrade and roll back

Before upgrading an existing database, read the target application's and registered plugins' release-specific upgrade notes. Include documented checksum changes, data prerequisites, and irreversible migrations in the recovery plan. Before the installer stops the application, inspect the target application's `db repair --dry-run --json` output using its supported CLI and deployment configuration, even when no historical correction is documented. This is a read-only checksum check: the installer's own `db apply --dry-run` discovers pending tasks but does not validate checksums, even under a strict checksum policy. If the selected installer cannot perform the required check or preparation, establish the supported maintenance procedure before proceeding with the upgrade.

When the checksum preview proposes changes, explain every migration or seed checksum difference before any actual repair; when it proposes none, skip repair. The installer applies migrations but does not automatically acknowledge changed historical checksums. Repair only updates history checksums; it does not change schema, fix partial tables, or replace a forward migration. Do not suppress drift by changing migration policy or repeatedly retrying the same archive.

Do not run actual repair before an ordinary installer upgrade. Its SQLite backup is taken after stopping the application and would already contain the new checksums, which the previous runtime can reject under `onChecksumMismatch: error` if the upgrade rolls back. A repair procedure must stop writers, back up the original history, perform the reviewed repair and migrations, and restore that same pre-repair backup before restarting the old runtime on failure. An extra manual backup alone does not change which backup automatic rollback restores. When the selected installer cannot coordinate that sequence, finish only the read-only checks and establish the supported maintenance procedure first.

Both stop the application, so the user decides:

1. An upgrade takes a new archive: `upgrade --dir <root> --archive <file> --json`. It must be the same application built for the same base path, and not an older version; the same version built again is a new release and deploys normally.
2. Run it without `--yes`. It answers `CONFIRMATION_REQUIRED` with `error.details.notes`: what will stop, what is backed up, and any Node major change. Relay those notes and wait for a clear yes before running it again with `--yes`. `success-noop` means that release is already running.
3. The installer backs up every SQLite database `config.yml` declares, plus `config.yml` and `app.env`, but not any other database: `BACKUP_REQUIRED` names those connections; have the user back them up first, then add `--backup-done`.
4. An upgrade keeps three releases, always including the new one and the one it came from, and prunes older ones once it succeeds; pass `--keep <n>` when the user wants more of them to stay available for rollback.
5. Read the outcome:
   - Exit 0: the new release passed its health check. Report `result.fromVersion`, `result.toVersion`, the release id `result.to`, `result.migrations` and `result.backup`, and name any release in `result.pruned`, which can no longer be rolled back to.
   - Exit 3: the previous release runs again. Report `error.message`, `error.details.log`, and whether the database was restored; an external database may still contain changes from the failed upgrade. Leave the next attempt to the user once the cause is known.
   - Exit 4: the application is down. Work through `error.suggestions` with the user, step by step.

`rollback --dir <root> --json` returns to the release the last upgrade came from, or to `--to <release id or version>`. When that upgrade migrated SQLite databases and the installer holds their backup, rolling back restores it and loses whatever was stored since; the confirmation notes say so, and the same relay-and-confirm step applies. External databases require a separate restore procedure: `--backup-done` does not make the installer restore them. If an irreversible migration made the schema incompatible with the previous runtime, returning to that runtime requires a compatible database backup too. `--no-restore` keeps the current databases; use it only when compatibility with the selected runtime is established.

## Recover an interrupted operation

`OPERATION_INTERRUPTED` from `upgrade`, or `pending` in `status`, means an earlier run stopped while the application was down. Plain `rollback` recovers, through the same confirmation: it undoes an interrupted upgrade, restoring the databases, and finishes an interrupted rollback.

## Change the origin or port

app-installer has no command for it. The origin, address and port live in `app.env` as `APP_PUBLIC_ORIGIN`, `APP_SERVER_HOST` and `APP_SERVER_PORT`. Before changing them, tell the user:

- the application will be at the new origin plus its base path;
- the application stops briefly while it restarts;
- a new port has to be free, or the application restarts into a crash loop that only `logs/app.err.log` explains, and a reverse proxy in front has to forward to it;
- `APP_BASE_PATH` cannot change this way: it is compiled into the client.

With their agreement, edit those three lines and nothing else, then run `pm2 restart <name>`, `<name>` being `name` in `status`. pm2 starts the application through `launcher.mjs`, which reads `app.env` on every start, so nothing has to be registered again. `status` afterwards reports the new `endpoints` and checks health at the address in `app.env`; for a new origin, have the user open `endpoints.url`.

## Keep the data intact

The root holds the only copy of the application's configuration, secrets and data. Change everything in it through app-installer, apart from the three `app.env` lines above, and leave the choice of deleting anything to the user. Keep the contents of `config.yml`, which holds the secrets, out of the conversation.

## Choose where the installer runs

When the user supplies an SSH server, keep the Agent, this Skill and the installer on the local machine. Read [Remote deployment](references/remote-deployment.md) before proceeding: it covers local orchestration, offline execution and recovery. The server needs no Agent, Skill or npm access. The `install`, `status`, `upgrade` and `rollback` guidance below still defines the lifecycle; run remote operations with the same SSH options and absolute remote `--dir`.

When the Agent is already on the application server, use the local commands below. An archive is built where the sources are, not in the production installation. If the source project is available locally, follow its `AGENTS.md` and `nocobase-deployment` Skill to build; otherwise obtain the archive from the user or CI. Do not build or run a development project on the production server.

## Build the archive

In the application project, whose own `AGENTS.md` and `nocobase-deployment` Skill are the authority on building:

```bash
APP_BASE_PATH=/crm pnpm build --target linux-x64 --node-version 24 --tar
```

- `--target` and `--node-version` describe the machine that will run it, not the one building it: `node -p "process.platform + '-' + process.arch"` and `node --version` there; Alpine takes a `-musl` target. The installer refuses an archive built for another machine and names the command that fits.
- `APP_BASE_PATH` is compiled into the client, `/main` when unset. The application is served there, and every later archive must be built for the same one.
- A database other than SQLite needs its driver in the project before the build, such as `pnpm add @nocobase/db-postgres@beta`: an archive carries only the drivers it was built with.

The archive is `storage/exports/dist.tar.gz`; the user copies it to the machine that runs NocoBase, for example `scp storage/exports/dist.tar.gz user@server:/tmp/crm.tar.gz`. `ARCHIVE_TOO_OLD` or `STORAGE_IN_RELEASE` means the project's NocoBase packages are older than the installer needs: upgrade them, build again, then retry.

## Install

### Every installation

1. Check the machine: `node --version` (24 or later) and `command -v pm2`, which finds pm2 without starting its daemon. pm2 4.3 or later has to be installed globally, `npm install -g pm2`; a copy fetched through `npx` breaks `pm2 startup`. Report what is missing with the command that installs it, and install nothing globally unless the user asks. On Windows, work in WSL.
2. Settle with the user: the target directory, new or empty, such as `/srv/nocobase/crm`; the public origin without the base path, such as `https://apps.example.com`, which may be left out for a machine reached only at `http://127.0.0.1:<port>`; whether a reverse proxy sits in front; the port, 13000 by default and different for every installation on the machine; and the database, SQLite by default.
3. It listens on `127.0.0.1`, which suits a reverse proxy on the same machine; when people reach it directly at `http://<address>:<port>`, add `--host 0.0.0.0` and use that address as the origin. For another database add `--dialect <dialect>`, the connection as `--set database.connections.main.host=…` and friends, and the password as `--set-from-env database.connections.main.password=<VARIABLE>` after the user has exported it; never put a password on the command line.
4. `PORT_IN_USE` names a free port in `error.details.freePort`; offer it rather than picking one silently.

### Run it

`install <dir> --archive <file> --origin <origin> --json`. It needs no pnpm, and finishes in a minute or two. The archive must carry the driver for `--dialect`, or the install stops with `DRIVER_MISSING` and the build command that fixes it.

### When it succeeds

When `result.started` is true, the installation answered its health check. Tell the user:

- `result.url`, and the first sign-in: `result.initialAdmin.username` or its `email`, with the password under `users.initialAdmin` in `config.yml`. When `result.initialAdmin.defaultPassword` is true, that password is still the `admin123` from `config.example.yml` and has to be changed after signing in; otherwise it is the one they set. The result never carries the password, and `config.yml` stays unread;
- each command in `result.nextCommands`: `pm2 startup` prints a command they run once with sudo, after which pm2 restores the process list the installer saved, so the installation comes back after a reboot;
- with a reverse proxy: it forwards to the installation's port with the WebSocket upgrade headers. Several installations behind one origin are routed by their base paths;
- anything in `warnings`.

A failed install before the switch leaves the target as it found it. What the failing step said is in `error.details`: `output` for unpacking the release, `stderr` and `stdout` when the release's own CLI printed no result; a failure that CLI reports itself keeps the CLI's own code, such as `CONFIG_INVALID`, and its `error.message` and `error.suggestions` say what was wrong. `START_FAILED` means installed but not running: show `error.details.log`.

## Several installations on one machine

Each application is installed once, in a directory of its own, with its own `--port`. The pm2 process name defaults to `nocobase-<directory name>`, so directories with different names never collide; two directories with the same name report `PM2_NAME_IN_USE` before anything is written, and `--name` gives the second its own.

## Status

`status --dir <root> --json` changes nothing. Report the application and `version`, `current` (the release id), `endpoints.url`, `health.ok`, `process`, and anything in `warnings`. `node.matches: false` means the machine's Node major changed since the release was built, and it will not load its native modules until a release built for this machine replaces it: the warning names the steps — a rebuilt archive and `upgrade --archive` — which go through the same stop, backup and confirmation as any upgrade. A non-null `pending` means an operation was interrupted; see below.

## Upgrade and roll back

Before upgrading an existing database, read the target application's and registered plugins' release-specific upgrade notes. Include documented checksum changes, data prerequisites, and irreversible migrations in the recovery plan. Before the installer stops the application, inspect the target application's `db repair --dry-run --json` output using its supported CLI and deployment configuration, even when no historical correction is documented. This is a read-only checksum check: the installer's own `db apply --dry-run` discovers pending tasks but does not validate checksums, even under a strict checksum policy. If the selected installer cannot perform the required check or preparation, establish the supported maintenance procedure before proceeding with the upgrade.

When the checksum preview proposes changes, explain every migration or seed checksum difference before any actual repair; when it proposes none, skip repair. The installer applies migrations but does not automatically acknowledge changed historical checksums. Repair only updates history checksums; it does not change schema, fix partial tables, or replace a forward migration. Do not suppress drift by changing migration policy or repeatedly retrying the same archive.

Do not run actual repair before an ordinary installer upgrade. Its SQLite backup is taken after stopping the application and would already contain the new checksums, which the previous runtime can reject under `onChecksumMismatch: error` if the upgrade rolls back. A repair procedure must stop writers, back up the original history, perform the reviewed repair and migrations, and restore that same pre-repair backup before restarting the old runtime on failure. An extra manual backup alone does not change which backup automatic rollback restores. When the selected installer cannot coordinate that sequence, finish only the read-only checks and establish the supported maintenance procedure first.

Both stop the application, so the user decides:

1. An upgrade takes a new archive: `upgrade --dir <root> --archive <file> --json`. It must be the same application built for the same base path, and not an older version; the same version built again is a new release and deploys normally.
2. Run it without `--yes`. It answers `CONFIRMATION_REQUIRED` with `error.details.notes`: what will stop, what is backed up, and any Node major change. Relay those notes and wait for a clear yes before running it again with `--yes`. `success-noop` means that release is already running.
3. The installer backs up every SQLite database `config.yml` declares, plus `config.yml` and `app.env`, but not any other database: `BACKUP_REQUIRED` names those connections; have the user back them up first, then add `--backup-done`.
4. An upgrade keeps three releases, always including the new one and the one it came from, and prunes older ones once it succeeds; pass `--keep <n>` when the user wants more of them to stay available for rollback.
5. Read the outcome:
   - Exit 0: the new release passed its health check. Report `result.fromVersion`, `result.toVersion`, the release id `result.to`, `result.migrations` and `result.backup`, and name any release in `result.pruned`, which can no longer be rolled back to.
   - Exit 3: the previous release runs again. Report `error.message`, `error.details.log`, and whether the database was restored; an external database may still contain changes from the failed upgrade. Leave the next attempt to the user once the cause is known.
   - Exit 4: the application is down. Work through `error.suggestions` with the user, step by step.

`rollback --dir <root> --json` returns to the release the last upgrade came from, or to `--to <release id or version>`. When that upgrade migrated SQLite databases and the installer holds their backup, rolling back restores it and loses whatever was stored since; the confirmation notes say so, and the same relay-and-confirm step applies. External databases require a separate restore procedure: `--backup-done` does not make the installer restore them. If an irreversible migration made the schema incompatible with the previous runtime, returning to that runtime requires a compatible database backup too. `--no-restore` keeps the current databases; use it only when compatibility with the selected runtime is established.

## Recover an interrupted operation

`OPERATION_INTERRUPTED` from `upgrade`, or `pending` in `status`, means an earlier run stopped while the application was down. Plain `rollback` recovers, through the same confirmation: it undoes an interrupted upgrade, restoring the databases, and finishes an interrupted rollback.

## Change the origin or port

app-installer has no command for it. The origin, address and port live in `app.env` as `APP_PUBLIC_ORIGIN`, `APP_SERVER_HOST` and `APP_SERVER_PORT`. Before changing them, tell the user:

- the application will be at the new origin plus its base path;
- the application stops briefly while it restarts;
- a new port has to be free, or the application restarts into a crash loop that only `logs/app.err.log` explains, and a reverse proxy in front has to forward to it;
- `APP_BASE_PATH` cannot change this way: it is compiled into the client.

With their agreement, edit those three lines and nothing else, then run `pm2 restart <name>`, `<name>` being `name` in `status`. pm2 starts the application through `launcher.mjs`, which reads `app.env` on every start, so nothing has to be registered again. `status` afterwards reports the new `endpoints` and checks health at the address in `app.env`; for a new origin, have the user open `endpoints.url`.

## Keep the data intact

The root holds the only copy of the application's configuration, secrets and data. Change everything in it through app-installer, apart from the three `app.env` lines above, and leave the choice of deleting anything to the user. Keep the contents of `config.yml`, which holds the secrets, out of the conversation.

name: nocobase-app-plugin-development
description: Migrate an older global NocoBase 3 plugin development Skill to the version supplied by the current App. Use when this legacy global entry is selected; it forwards to project guidance and contains no plugin implementation instructions.
---

# Use the project's plugin development Skill

The complete `nocobase-app-plugin-development` Skill is maintained in `@nocobase/app-skills` and delivered with compatible App releases. This global entry is a migration bridge, not an implementation guide. Do not assume that an installed App already includes the new Skill or that a project Skill automatically overrides a global one.

Find the owning App from the current directory and its ancestors, read its `AGENTS.md`, then open `<app-root>/.agents/skills/nocobase-app-plugin-development/SKILL.md` by its explicit path. Resolve symlinks and confirm this is a different file from this bridge. Do not invoke this Skill again by name. Follow the complete project Skill and its references for implementation.

If that file is missing, check whether the installed `@nocobase/app-skills` actually ships it before running `pnpm nocobase skills sync` from the App root. If it does not, do not repeatedly sync or install a newer `app-skills` in isolation. Explain that a compatible App release is required, read the project's `nocobase-app-upgrade` Skill, and upgrade only within the user's requested scope. Until a compatible release is available, use the installed App's guidance and public package declarations; report missing guidance rather than inventing APIs. Do not remove an existing full global copy before a working project replacement is available.

For work explicitly in the NocoBase source repository, read `packages/app/app-skills/skills/nocobase-app-plugin-development/SKILL.md` and `.agents/rules/plugin-development.md` from that repository root. No source download is required for an App. With no App, use the available `nocobase-create-app` entry first.

After the project replacement is verified, retire this exact global installation and its Agent discovery links as part of the agreed migration. Inspect real paths, preserve custom content outside Skill discovery directories, and never follow a global symlink to delete a source checkout or project copy. Do not remove the differently named V2 Skill or unrelated Skills. Report any remaining global entries and start a new Agent session after cleanup; this session can continue by reading the project file directly. Detailed migration guidance ships with the target release's `nocobase-app-upgrade` Skill.

skills.body:
---
name: nocobase-create-app
description: Create a NocoBase 3 project to develop, locally, with `pnpm create @nocobase/app@beta`, configure it with `pnpm nocobase config init`, `config set` and `config check`, start it, and hand over to the application's own guidance. Use when the user asks to install, create, set up or try NocoBase to develop with, and the working directory holds no NocoBase application yet. Not for deploying to production, which belongs to the `nocobase-app-installer` Skill. Not for NocoBase 2 or the `nb` CLI, and not for work inside an existing application, which carries its own AGENTS.md and Skills.
---

# Create a NocoBase 3 application

This Skill gets a new project created, configured and running locally: source code to develop, not a built application to deploy. It does not describe how to develop one: the moment the application exists, its own `AGENTS.md` and `.agents/skills/` take over. Those match the version that was installed and this Skill does not, so prefer them wherever the two differ.

## Before you start

- If the working directory already holds a NocoBase application — a `package.json` with a `nocobase` field, next to an `AGENTS.md` — do not use this Skill. Read that `AGENTS.md` and continue from it.
- NocoBase 3 is created with `pnpm create @nocobase/app@beta`. Never fall back to NocoBase 2 instructions or the `nb` CLI, including when a package cannot be found; see Troubleshooting instead.
- Check the request is this Skill's. A project is source code someone changes, developed locally; an installation is a built NocoBase that only runs, usually in production, and belongs to `nocobase-app-installer`:

  | The user asks to                                  | Skill                                                                   |
  | ------------------------------------------------- | ----------------------------------------------------------------------- |
  | Install, create, set up or try NocoBase, to develop with | This one                                                         |
  | Deploy an application to production or a server   | `nocobase-app-installer`, `--archive`                                   |

  Hand a request to deploy over to `nocobase-app-installer`, and stop here.
- On Windows, work in WSL. The commands below assume a POSIX shell such as Bash; the subshell and the inline environment variable do not work in PowerShell or cmd.
- Check `node --version` (24 or later) and `pnpm --version` (11). If either is missing or does not match, stop before creating anything and tell the user:
  - which tool is missing or which version was found, and which version is required;
  - the command to install it on their operating system, preferring a version manager they already use, such as `nvm install 24` or `fnm install 24`, and for pnpm `corepack enable && corepack prepare pnpm@11 --activate` or `npm install -g pnpm@11`;
  - to open a new shell afterwards, so the new version is on `PATH`.

  Do not install either yourself unless the user asks. Check both versions again before continuing.
- Create the application in the directory the user names, or in the current directory when it is empty. The directory must be new or empty, and its name becomes the application name: it starts with a lowercase letter or digit and contains only lowercase letters, digits, dots, dashes and underscores. If the directory is not empty or its name is invalid, ask the user for another one. Never overwrite files, and never create a nested project and move its files afterwards.

## Choose the template

Use Default for an ordinary application, Examples for exploring bundled examples, and `multi-portal` when the user asks for one application with multiple business entry points. Use `multi-app` when the user asks for a Main application that manages independent child applications, and `sub-app` for a child application that such a Main deploys (see Continue by creating a child application). Multi-portal, multi-app and sub-app are commercial Pro templates. Multi-portal is not a tenant or process isolation mechanism. Keep the user's explicit template choice.

For Default and Examples, continue with Create below. For multi-portal, multi-app or sub-app, follow the commercial registry authentication steps below, verify access to the selected template package, then use that template's creation command instead of the public-registry command below.

### Commercial multi-portal template

The template, portal management plugin and portal generator are commercial packages downloaded from `https://pkg-v3.nocobase.com/`. Before creating files, check the existing login and access to the requested version or channel:

```bash
npm whoami --registry=https://pkg-v3.nocobase.com/
npm view @nocobase/app-template-multi-portal@beta version --registry=https://pkg-v3.nocobase.com/
```

Reuse valid credentials. If authentication is missing or expired, use the host's secure secret-input tool when available, or have the user log in through their terminal:

```bash
pnpm login --registry=https://pkg-v3.nocobase.com/ --scope=@nocobase
```

This intentionally configures the `@nocobase` scope for the commercial registry. The password prompt takes the registry read token. Do not ask for the token in chat, print credentials, put them in command arguments, or copy them into project files. For secure file delivery, create an isolated npm user config outside the project (directory mode 700, file mode 600), containing the scoped registry and host-scoped token. Pass its path through `NPM_CONFIG_USERCONFIG` to every download/install command; never print its contents or change the global login. Remove that temporary copy after verification, and explain that future installs need the user's own login. After login, check package access again. A successful `whoami` alone does not establish download permission. On 401/403, resolve authentication or package access; on 404 or a missing channel, confirm the package/version is published and accessible. Stop creation if unavailable; do not silently select Default or claim an unreleased package is available. For an explicitly requested local preview registry, use that registry and its test credentials instead.

After access succeeds, create from the parent directory:

```bash
(cd <parent-directory> && PNPM_CONFIG_MINIMUM_RELEASE_AGE=0 NOCOBASE_REGISTRY=https://pkg-v3.nocobase.com/ npm_config_registry=https://registry.npmjs.org pnpm create @nocobase/app@beta <name> --template=multi-portal --template-tag=beta --json)
```

`multi-portal` resolves to `@nocobase/app-template-multi-portal` and honors `--template-tag`. With a create-app version that predates the alias, use `--template=@nocobase/app-template-multi-portal@beta` instead; a full package specifier ignores `--template-tag`, so include the channel or explicit version in the specifier. Reuse the user's chosen registry/version rather than replacing it with these defaults. Registry selection is explicit even after login because create-app otherwise defaults to public npm. The generated `.npmrc` contains the registry URL, not credentials.

Create-app `0.1.0-beta.36` includes the private-registry installation fix: `NOCOBASE_REGISTRY` selects the template and the generated `@nocobase` scope, while third-party dependencies use the package manager's default registry. Keep that default public (or use the user's chosen public mirror); do not set it to a NocoBase-only private registry. The command installs dependencies automatically. Confirm `ok: true` and `result.dependenciesInstalled: true`, read the generated `AGENTS.md`, then continue with Configure and Start. Postinstall synchronizes Skills; run `pnpm nocobase skills sync` only if synchronization failed or its files are missing.

For an explicitly selected older create-app release such as `0.1.0-beta.35`, use `--no-install`, then run the following in the generated app. Also use this recovery command when a previous attempt already created files but failed at dependency installation; do not create the project again:

```bash
(cd <parent-directory>/<name> && PNPM_CONFIG_MINIMUM_RELEASE_AGE=0 npm_config_registry=https://registry.npmjs.org pnpm install)
```

Reuse the same authentication configuration for recovery. With `--no-install`, `ok: true` means scaffolding only and `dependenciesInstalled` is false. Confirm the project `.npmrc` has the intended `@nocobase:registry` URL without credentials. Once created, use the application's own `AGENTS.md`, `.agents/rules/multi-portal.md` and installed Skills for portal development. The portal command is `pnpm create @nocobase/portal`; generated portals start uninstalled and an authorized administrator installs them through System settings → Portals. Do not use `pnpm create:module` or replace business authorization with a grant to all users.

### Commercial multi-app template

`multi-app` resolves to `@nocobase/app-template-multi-app` from the Pro registry and honors `--template-tag`. It creates **Main only**, with application management capabilities. It does not generate `apps/sub` or require an `apps/` directory; independent child applications are added on demand.

Reuse the commercial registry login and scoped authentication procedure above, but verify the multi-app package itself before creating files:

```bash
npm view @nocobase/app-template-multi-app@beta version --registry=https://pkg-v3.nocobase.com/
```

Check the selected generator's `--help` for `multi-app` in the supported template names. Once package access and alias support are confirmed, create Main from the parent directory:

```bash
(cd <parent-directory> && PNPM_CONFIG_MINIMUM_RELEASE_AGE=0 NOCOBASE_REGISTRY=https://pkg-v3.nocobase.com/ npm_config_registry=https://registry.npmjs.org pnpm create @nocobase/app@beta <name> --template multi-app --template-tag beta --json)
```

A generator without this alias, including create-app `0.1.0-beta.36`, can use `--template=@nocobase/app-template-multi-app@beta` instead; omit `--template-tag` because the package specifier already selects the channel. This still requires a published, accessible template. If the package or requested version is unavailable, report the blocker rather than substituting Default. For an explicitly requested unreleased preview, use the actual packed template artifact provided for that preview. Reuse the user's selected registry and version.

Confirm `ok: true` and `result.dependenciesInstalled: true`, read the generated `AGENTS.md`, then follow Configure and Start below. Once Main is running, offer the child-creation guide below before the final handover. Configure an available Releases App Host before creating managed instances; starting Main alone does not enable child deployment.

### Continue by creating a child application

After Main is configured and running, ask whether the user wants to create a child now. Do not create one automatically. If they decline, finish with Main's handover. If they agree, offer `<main-directory>/packages/child-app` as the default and accept a user-specified directory; resolve relative paths from Main. Reuse explicit choices instead of asking again. Require a new or empty target and never overwrite an existing application.

Before creation, ask whether the child needs platform-wide SSO. Independent login is the default. Selecting SSO authorizes installing and configuring the commercial `@nocobase/app-plugin-platform-sso` package; merely requesting a child does not. Reuse the commercial registry authentication procedure and verify access to a compatible plugin version before installation. If access or required SSO configuration is unavailable, report the blocker rather than silently changing the login choice.

When the user selected SSO, prefer the commercial `sub-app` template (`@nocobase/app-template-sub-app`), which already registers platform SSO and preinstalls the `deploy` CLI extension: verify it with `npm view @nocobase/app-template-sub-app@beta version --registry=https://pkg-v3.nocobase.com/` and check that the generator's `--help` lists `sub-app`, then use `--template sub-app` with `NOCOBASE_REGISTRY=https://pkg-v3.nocobase.com/` in the command below and skip the separate SSO plugin installation. If the template or alias is unavailable, use the Default procedure below. Otherwise create the child as an ordinary Default application, not another multi-app Main. Create its parent directory when needed and run from that parent with the target's basename; do not pass a slash-containing path or `.` as the application name. For the default location:

```bash
mkdir -p <main-directory>/packages
(cd <main-directory>/packages && PNPM_CONFIG_MINIMUM_RELEASE_AGE=0 pnpm create @nocobase/app@beta child-app --template default --template-tag beta --no-install --json)
```

Use `--no-install` so the workspace boundary can be checked before dependency installation; `dependenciesInstalled: false` is expected at this step. Main's default workspace includes `packages/*`. For a child nested under Main, preserve existing workspace settings and exclude that exact child from Main's `pnpm-workspace.yaml` package globs (for the default directory, append `!packages/child-app`). Keep the child's generated `pnpm-workspace.yaml` and its own lockfile; do not add it as a Main dependency. From the child directory, verify `pnpm root -w` points to the child's `node_modules` before running `pnpm install`. For a custom location, check any enclosing workspace and establish the same independent boundary. Do not relocate the user's requested target silently.

Read the child's own `AGENTS.md`, install dependencies there, and follow Configure and Start for that child. Keep its configuration, database and storage independent from Main, and select a different local port. Keep child source and runtime files out of Main's deployment archive; Main consumes the child's separately built archive.

If the user selected SSO, configure the child's `@nocobase` registry and reuse secure credentials before running `pnpm add @nocobase/app-plugin-platform-sso@<compatible-version>` in the child. `NOCOBASE_REGISTRY` alone does not configure `pnpm add`. Synchronize Skills if the installed plugin's guidance is missing, then follow `nocobase-app-plugin-platform-sso` for server/client/config registration and login verification, and `nocobase-app-plugin-multi-app` in Main for the platform-side setup. Installation alone does not enable SSO. Resolve the platform issuer, child origin/callback, application/client identity and securely supplied credentials; retain local recovery login unless the user explicitly requests a different policy. Without SSO, keep ordinary local authentication and do not install that plugin.

Verify child startup and, when selected, the actual SSO flow before reporting them as working. Report Main and child directories, URLs, selected login mode and any remaining setup. # Create a NocoBase 3 application

This Skill gets a new project created, configured and running locally: source code to develop, not a built application to deploy. It does not describe how to develop one: the moment the application exists, its own `AGENTS.md` and `.agents/skills/` take over. Those match the version that was installed and this Skill does not, so prefer them wherever the two differ.

## Before you start

- If the working directory already holds a NocoBase application — a `package.json` with a `nocobase` field, next to an `AGENTS.md` — do not use this Skill. Read that `AGENTS.md` and continue from it.
- NocoBase 3 is created with `pnpm create @nocobase/app@beta`. Never fall back to NocoBase 2 instructions or the `nb` CLI, including when a package cannot be found; see Troubleshooting instead.
- Check the request is this Skill's. A project is source code someone changes, developed locally; an installation is a built NocoBase that only runs, usually in production, and belongs to `nocobase-app-installer`:

  | The user asks to                                  | Skill                                                                   |
  | ------------------------------------------------- | ----------------------------------------------------------------------- |
  | Install, create, set up or try NocoBase, to develop with | This one                                                         |
  | Deploy an application to production or a server   | `nocobase-app-installer`, `--archive`                                   |

  Hand a request to deploy over to `nocobase-app-installer`, and stop here.
- On Windows, work in WSL. The commands below assume a POSIX shell such as Bash; the subshell and the inline environment variable do not work in PowerShell or cmd.
- Check `node --version` (24 or later) and `pnpm --version` (11). If either is missing or does not match, stop before creating anything and tell the user:
  - which tool is missing or which version was found, and which version is required;
  - the command to install it on their operating system, preferring a version manager they already use, such as `nvm install 24` or `fnm install 24`, and for pnpm `corepack enable && corepack prepare pnpm@11 --activate` or `npm install -g pnpm@11`;
  - to open a new shell afterwards, so the new version is on `PATH`.

  Do not install either yourself unless the user asks. Check both versions again before continuing.
- Create the application in the directory the user names, or in the current directory when it is empty. The directory must be new or empty, and its name becomes the application name: it starts with a lowercase letter or digit and contains only lowercase letters, digits, dots, dashes and underscores. If the directory is not empty or its name is invalid, ask the user for another one. Never overwrite files, and never create a nested project and move its files afterwards.

## Choose the template

Use Default for an ordinary application, Examples for exploring bundled examples, and `multi-portal` when the user asks for one application with multiple business entry points. Use `multi-app` when the user asks for a Main application that manages independent child applications, and `sub-app` for a child application that such a Main deploys (see Continue by creating a child application). Multi-portal, multi-app and sub-app are commercial Pro templates. Multi-portal is not a tenant or process isolation mechanism. Keep the user's explicit template choice.

For Default and Examples, continue with Create below. For multi-portal, multi-app or sub-app, follow the commercial registry authentication steps below, verify access to the selected template package, then use that template's creation command instead of the public-registry command below.

### Commercial multi-portal template

The template, portal management plugin and portal generator are commercial packages downloaded from `https://pkg-v3.nocobase.com/`. Before creating files, check the existing login and access to the requested version or channel:

```bash
npm whoami --registry=https://pkg-v3.nocobase.com/
npm view @nocobase/app-template-multi-portal@beta version --registry=https://pkg-v3.nocobase.com/
```

Reuse valid credentials. If authentication is missing or expired, use the host's secure secret-input tool when available, or have the user log in through their terminal:

```bash
pnpm login --registry=https://pkg-v3.nocobase.com/ --scope=@nocobase
```

This intentionally configures the `@nocobase` scope for the commercial registry. The password prompt takes the registry read token. Do not ask for the token in chat, print credentials, put them in command arguments, or copy them into project files. For secure file delivery, create an isolated npm user config outside the project (directory mode 700, file mode 600), containing the scoped registry and host-scoped token. Pass its path through `NPM_CONFIG_USERCONFIG` to every download/install command; never print its contents or change the global login. Remove that temporary copy after verification, and explain that future installs need the user's own login. After login, check package access again. A successful `whoami` alone does not establish download permission. On 401/403, resolve authentication or package access; on 404 or a missing channel, confirm the package/version is published and accessible. Stop creation if unavailable; do not silently select Default or claim an unreleased package is available. For an explicitly requested local preview registry, use that registry and its test credentials instead.

After access succeeds, create from the parent directory:

```bash
(cd <parent-directory> && PNPM_CONFIG_MINIMUM_RELEASE_AGE=0 NOCOBASE_REGISTRY=https://pkg-v3.nocobase.com/ npm_config_registry=https://registry.npmjs.org pnpm create @nocobase/app@beta <name> --template=multi-portal --template-tag=beta --json)
```

`multi-portal` resolves to `@nocobase/app-template-multi-portal` and honors `--template-tag`. With a create-app version that predates the alias, use `--template=@nocobase/app-template-multi-portal@beta` instead; a full package specifier ignores `--template-tag`, so include the channel or explicit version in the specifier. Reuse the user's chosen registry/version rather than replacing it with these defaults. Registry selection is explicit even after login because create-app otherwise defaults to public npm. The generated `.npmrc` contains the registry URL, not credentials.

Create-app `0.1.0-beta.36` includes the private-registry installation fix: `NOCOBASE_REGISTRY` selects the template and the generated `@nocobase` scope, while third-party dependencies use the package manager's default registry. Keep that default public (or use the user's chosen public mirror); do not set it to a NocoBase-only private registry. The command installs dependencies automatically. Confirm `ok: true` and `result.dependenciesInstalled: true`, read the generated `AGENTS.md`, then continue with Configure and Start. Postinstall synchronizes Skills; run `pnpm nocobase skills sync` only if synchronization failed or its files are missing.

For an explicitly selected older create-app release such as `0.1.0-beta.35`, use `--no-install`, then run the following in the generated app. Also use this recovery command when a previous attempt already created files but failed at dependency installation; do not create the project again:

```bash
(cd <parent-directory>/<name> && PNPM_CONFIG_MINIMUM_RELEASE_AGE=0 npm_config_registry=https://registry.npmjs.org pnpm install)
```

Reuse the same authentication configuration for recovery. With `--no-install`, `ok: true` means scaffolding only and `dependenciesInstalled` is false. Confirm the project `.npmrc` has the intended `@nocobase:registry` URL without credentials. Once created, use the application's own `AGENTS.md`, `.agents/rules/multi-portal.md` and installed Skills for portal development. The portal command is `pnpm create @nocobase/portal`; generated portals start uninstalled and an authorized administrator installs them through System settings → Portals. Do not use `pnpm create:module` or replace business authorization with a grant to all users.

### Commercial multi-app template

`multi-app` resolves to `@nocobase/app-template-multi-app` from the Pro registry and honors `--template-tag`. It creates **Main only**, with application management capabilities. It does not generate `apps/sub` or require an `apps/` directory; independent child applications are added on demand.

Reuse the commercial registry login and scoped authentication procedure above, but verify the multi-app package itself before creating files:

```bash
npm view @nocobase/app-template-multi-app@beta version --registry=https://pkg-v3.nocobase.com/
```

Check the selected generator's `--help` for `multi-app` in the supported template names. Once package access and alias support are confirmed, create Main from the parent directory:

